title: Logo files a client actually needs
metaTitle: The logo files a delivery needs
excerpt: Deliver an SVG for the web, a PNG on a transparent ground, and a version for dark backgrounds. A hundred exports and no instruction is not a delivery.
alt: Five people working on laptops around a wooden table. The shared table fits a piece about logo files a team can pick up and use.
caption: Name the files for the job, then stop. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: Which logo files should a delivery include?
faqs.answer: An SVG for the website, a PNG on a transparent background for decks and forms, and a light version of both for dark backgrounds. Add a favicon set if you are shipping the site. Skip the pile of every possible width. Extra files without a job get used in the wrong place.

faqs.question: Why is SVG the file for the web?
faqs.answer: It stays sharp at any size and can be colored by the page when you build it that way. Outline the lettering so the wordmark does not depend on a font installed on someone else's computer. Use the PNG when a tool refuses SVG, and export that PNG large enough to scale down.

faqs.question: How do you keep an old logo from coming back?
faqs.answer: Keep the latest files in one place the team already opens, with a date and a line that says earlier email attachments are retired. Name files for their job, such as logo-on-dark, and lead with five lines of use. A zip in an old thread will otherwise outlive the correction.

markdown:
Logo file formats are a short list: an SVG for the web, a PNG on a transparent ground, and a version that works on a dark background. A hundred exports and no instruction is not a delivery. The client should be able to pick a file without asking which one is "the real logo."

Name the files for the job. Put them in one folder. Write five lines at the top that say when to use each. That is the delivery. The rest is archive.

## The three files people actually open

SVG for the web. It stays sharp at any size, it can follow a text color when you build it that way, and it is the file the site should use in the header, the footer, and the favicon source. Outline the type. Do not depend on a font being installed on the visitor's machine. A wordmark that looks right only on your laptop is a broken logo everywhere else.

PNG on a transparent ground, at a size that survives a slide and a document. This is the file a founder drops into a deck, a proposal, and a partner form that refuses SVG. Export it large enough that they are scaling down, not up. A 200-pixel PNG that gets stretched across a title slide looks soft, and they will blame the logo rather than the file.

A version that works on a dark background. If the primary mark is dark ink, it will vanish on the dark paper, on a photograph, and in a footer that is not white. Ship a light version, with the same proportions, on its own transparent PNG and its own SVG. Do not tell them to "just put a white box behind it" unless a white box is actually part of the mark. Most of the time it is a patch, and it will be cropped badly.

Those three cover the week after delivery. If you stop there and the instructions are clear, you have done the useful part. Extra sizes can exist. They do not lead the folder.

## What else is worth including, and what is noise

A favicon set is worth including if you built the site, or if they are about to. The browser icon, the apple touch icon, and a simple manifest icon. Square, legible at 16 pixels, often a reduced mark rather than the full wordmark. A wordmark that cannot be read at that size should not be forced into the tab. Write that in the note so nobody "fixes" it later by shrinking the whole logo.

A single-color version belongs in the folder when the mark is ever embroidered, stamped, or limited to one ink. It is the same drawing, one fill. It is not a new idea.

Horizontal and stacked versions belong only if both are real, designed layouts. A stacked version made by a hurried resize on the morning of a conference is how the logo grows a second personality. If you include both, label them `logo-horizontal` and `logo-stacked`, and say where each goes. Header versus a square avatar, for example. If one of them is awkward, do not include it "in case."

What you can leave out: forty PNGs at every width from 50 to 2000, a JPEG on a white rectangle, a PDF with the logo floating in an unlabeled artboard, and a source file with hidden layers named Final, Final2, and Use This One. Keep the source, one file, for the people who will edit with you. Do not make the source the thing a founder is supposed to open on a Tuesday.

JPEG is the wrong default. It throws away the edge and it cannot be transparent. The only JPEG you might add is a social image that already includes a background you designed, and that file is a social card, not the logo. Name it as a card so it is not reused in the header.

## Name the files, and write the five lines

A folder called `logo` with three names beats a folder called `export-final` with thirty. Use plain names: `logo.svg`, `logo.png`, `logo-on-dark.svg`, `logo-on-dark.png`. Add `mark.svg` only if the symbol is meant to be used without the word. If the symbol should not appear alone, do not export it. Someone will use whatever you export.

The five lines sit in a `README` or at the top of the brand page:

- SVG on the website.
- PNG for decks and tools that will not take SVG.
- The on-dark files for dark backgrounds and photos.
- Do not recolor, outline, or add a shadow.
- Do not redraw the wordmark in a font you happen to have installed.

That is enough instruction for a founder and for a teammate who was not in the room. Google's guidance on people-first content asks whether someone can leave having learned enough to achieve their goal, without having to search again for a better explanation. A logo folder passes that test when the right file can be chosen from the names and the five lines alone. A folder that requires a meeting to interpret has not been delivered yet. See [Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content). A brand book of forty pages that hides this list on page twelve will not be opened on the day they need the file. Lead with the list. Put the story of the mark after it, if you have one worth keeping.

Show a small sheet of correct and incorrect uses. The logo on paper, the logo on the dark version, too small to read, stretched, recolored, and sitting on a busy photo with no room. Six pictures teach more than a paragraph of "clear space." If you specify clear space, specify it as a fraction of the mark, once, and show it. A number with no picture will be ignored.

## Color, space, and the versions you refuse

The logo uses the ink color, or a single specified color, on paper. It uses the light version on dark. It does not get a gradient, a new accent, or a seasonal recolor unless you design that recolor and file it beside the originals with a date. A recolor in a slide is how the mark forks.

Clear space can be simple: at least the height of the symbol, on every side, before another logo or a headline collides with it. If the header of the site cannot afford that much air, design the header properly rather than publishing a rule the site itself breaks. Rules the site breaks will be broken everywhere, with a clear conscience.

Minimum size is the size at which the word is still a word. Set it by looking, at 100 percent, on a phone and on a slide. Write the pixel height for screen and the millimeter height for print if they truly print. If they do not print, skip the millimeters. Unused rules train people to skip the rest of the page.

Do not provide a "knockout" version that is just the dark file with a multiply blend mode and a prayer. Export the pixels. Blend modes depend on the software the next person may not have.

A partner lockup, your logo beside someone else's, is a separate file if it happens often. Build it once, with the clear space decided, and store it. Letting every partner page invent the spacing is how the logo gets a new proportion each month.

## Where the files live after the meeting

Email is a poor shelf. The zip attached to the thread will be old the moment you fix a curve. The latest files belong where the client already goes for brand material. On a Hanabi project, that place is the client portal: the logo files, the one-page note, and the date they were updated. The portal holds the current version so a teammate who joins later does not inherit the zip.

Tell them what replaced what. "Use the files in the portal. The email from March is retired." A single sentence prevents the old wordmark from returning on a one-pager someone saved.

If you change the mark later, do not overwrite silently. Add the date to the folder or the page, keep one previous set labeled previous, and say why the new files exist in one line. People who already downloaded the PNG will keep using it until the note is easier to find than their downloads folder. Make the note easier to find.

The website should use the SVG you delivered, not a PNG screenshot of it, and not a new tracing. If the site and the folder disagree, fix the site. Two official logos is how a small company starts to look careless at the exact size where people are trying to trust it.

## A check on the day you hand it over

Open the folder as if you were the founder, on a machine that does not have the design app installed.

- You can find the SVG, the transparent PNG, and the on-dark pair without a guide.
- The five lines are at the top.
- The PNG looks sharp when placed large in a slide.
- The on-dark files are visible on black and on a photograph.
- Nothing in the folder invites a use you meant to forbid.
- You can say, in one sentence, where the latest files will live next month.

If any export requires you to explain it in person, the export is not done. Add the line, or remove the file.

The folder still needs a home after the call ends. [A brand kit inside the client portal](/blog/a-brand-kit-inside-the-client-portal) is the next piece. The files, the rules, and the latest version should live where the client can find them. A zip in a thread is how the old logo comes back.

When you want that short delivery put together and filed where the team will actually look, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The logo is the files they can use, not the folder of everything the tools could export.
